title: The Letter of James
lead: The Letter of James is a short wisdom letter of the New Testament, sent by "James, a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" to "the twelve tribes in the Dispersion". It is known for its teaching that "faith without works is dead", its closeness to the Sermon on the Mount, its warnings about the tongue and wealth, and its instructions on prayer and anointing the sick.

sections.b: James calls scattered, mostly poor believers to a faith that is whole: joy and endurance in trials, wisdom asked of God, no favoritism toward the rich, faith shown in works, a tamed tongue, wisdom from above, humility before God, patience until the Lord's coming, and prayer for the sick and the wandering. It has the form of a letter but the voice of a Jewish sage.

Tradition names James the brother of Jesus, head of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 1:19; Acts 15:13), who was stoned in Jerusalem about AD 62. Many critical scholars think a later writer used his name; others think his teaching was collected and edited by his followers. The early church was slow to accept the letter: Eusebius counted it among the disputed books, though read in many churches.

James 2:24 ("it is by works that a person is justified, and not by faith alone") is set beside Romans 3:28 ("a person is justified by faith, apart from works of the law"). Both use Abraham. Most churches read the two as answering different questions; how they fit together is one of the great dividing questions between the Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions. See the topic on justification.
